title: Wheelwright Pian and Duke Huan
text:
Duke Huan was reading a book up in his hall, while below, in the courtyard, a wheelwright named Pian was chiseling a wheel. Pian put down his tools, went up the steps and asked the duke what he was reading.

"The words of the sages," said the duke. "Are the sages still alive?" asked Pian. "They are dead." "Then what you are reading is only the dregs of the ancients."

The duke was angry. How dare a wheelwright comment on his reading? "If you can explain yourself, well and good. If not, you die."

Pian answered from his own trade. When he cut a wheel, if he worked too slowly the chisel slid and did not bite, and if he worked too fast it jammed and stuck. Not too slow and not too fast: he got it in his hand and felt it in his heart. He could not put it into words. There was a knack to it, but he could not teach it even to his own son, and his son could not learn it from him. That was why, at seventy, he was still making wheels himself. The ancients, he said, died along with what they could not pass on, so what the duke was reading was only their dregs.
lesson: Books and reports cannot give you the judgment that comes from doing the work. If you lead people who make things, spend time where the work happens and learn from those whose hands know it.
